## What HEY lets you do outside a normal phone app

HEY’s defining ambition is that intelligence does not stop at the chat box. It can extend into the computer, browser, files, displays, trusted devices and physical interaction surfaces—while remaining permissioned and visible.

Control supported computers with pointer, keyboard, windows, apps, files, clipboard, screenshots and terminal actions under explicit permissions.

Use HEY Live to understand a selected monitor, app window, screen region or camera and guide the user with overlays, labels, arrows and step markers.

Keep timers, schedules, workflows, notifications, research and trusted background helpers running after the main window closes when the OS allows it.

Use a native compact Dynamic Island-like surface on desktop and legitimate equivalents on mobile platforms for status, approvals, timers, voice and progress.

Move conversations, missions, files and artifacts between trusted devices through Device Fabric and handoff checkpoints.

Use another trusted phone/tablet as a camera, confirmation device, presentation remote or companion while a desktop acts as the workstation.

Run local file search, selected local models, local computer control and cached memory during limited or offline operation.

Use optional gestures to summon HEY, select, drag, navigate, confirm/reject and control media or supported system actions.

Turn research or files directly into documents, presentations, worksheets, flashcards, media and structured artifacts rather than copying between separate apps.

Allow long-running missions to use cloud continuation or another trusted device when the local machine sleeps, where infrastructure and platform policy permit it.

### Examples of end-to-end “outside the app” workflows

Fix something on the computer: The user says “the download is broken.” HEY inspects the active window, asks for any required permission, checks the download state, identifies the cause, guides or acts, verifies the resulting file and returns an action receipt.

Continue a mission on another device: A desktop research mission reaches a point where the user leaves. HEY checkpoints the task and hands supervision to a trusted phone; later the final artifact appears back on the desktop with the same mission timeline.

Use the tablet as a visual companion: The desktop remains the compute/work device while a tablet shows a reference, camera feed, presentation controls or confirmation prompt.

Ambient voice without a full window: On a supported native platform, HEY can remain available through a tray helper, wake phrase and compact island; the full app opens only when the task needs richer context.

Gesture-assisted control: With explicit camera permission and visible sensing, a user can summon HEY, move/select items, pause media, confirm/reject or navigate supported interfaces using learned gestures.

Project-aware creation across apps: A user selects source files, asks for a campaign, and HEY produces copy, visuals, a presentation and video storyboard using the same Project DNA and approved brand rules rather than re-prompting each tool.

## What becomes newly possible or dramatically easier with HEY

Many individual ingredients exist in separate products. HEY’s differentiation is the integration: shared context, governed memory, cross-device continuity, verified action, creation systems and a single trust model. The following are the workflows HEY is designed to make practical in one system.

One relationship instead of separate assistants — HEY unifies chat, voice, Live, compact UI, memory, projects and devices around the same user and task context.

Memory that behaves like governed infrastructure — Cosmos is not just a chat-history search. It models provenance, confidence, privacy, contradictions, expiry, graph relationships and user approval.

Project DNA as a consistency engine — Brand, terminology, identity, accepted/rejected examples and design rules can persist across months of work and across output formats.

Pinpoint editing across modalities — The same “change only this” philosophy applies to text, code, images, layouts, audio, video and structured artifacts.

Action with verifiable state — HEY is designed to separate an intended action from an actually verified result, reducing the common assistant failure of claiming success after only generating instructions.

AI that can exist outside its main window — Background helpers, Dynamic Island, notifications, device handoff and native adapters let HEY participate in the user’s workflow without demanding a full-screen chat.

Capability creation without unsafe self-authority — Forge can design and test new capabilities, but permissions and high-risk installation remain governed by the user/security model.

Cross-device roles rather than duplicate apps — Each device can contribute what it is good at: screen/keyboard, camera, portability, confirmation, presentation control or compute.

One creation system from source to final artifact — Research, image/video/audio creation, presentations, documents and motion graphics share Project DNA, provenance, versions and verification.

A personal operating policy — Modes, privacy routing, provider budgets, notification caps, quiet hours and permission preferences let HEY behave differently without forcing the user to micromanage every request.

## System architecture and execution model

### Canonical execution flow

1. User intent / trigger

2. Context assembly with privacy filters

3. Capability lookup

4. Platform/provider availability

5. Trusted identity and authorization

6. Confirmation gate when required

7. Agent/tool/workflow execution

8. Verification

9. Normalized result

10. Audit + provenance + memory update + UI receipt

### Non-negotiable security boundaries

Client-supplied role, plan, entitlement or permission data is never authoritative at a sensitive execution boundary.

Agents, workflows, Forge artifacts and automations cannot grant themselves permissions or bypass confirmation policy.

Secrets stay server-side or in appropriate secure native storage; service-role secrets are never shipped in browser-visible variables.

High-impact operations must expose scope, risk and expected effect before action when meaningful.

Unsupported capabilities fail closed instead of returning fake success.

Prompt/tool output is treated as untrusted input when it can influence browser/computer control or other external actions.

Minimum necessary context is sent to providers; sensitive projects may require local-only routing.

Emergency Stop should be able to halt autonomous/high-risk actions while preserving read-only diagnostics.

### Provider routing

The launch router is free-first: local, free or free-tier paths are preferred when they satisfy quality and privacy needs. Paid adapters may be ready but disabled until configured. Routing can consider modality, task class, model capability, health, latency, cost, privacy, plan and explicit user choice. Circuit breakers and fallback prevent one failing provider from freezing the whole product.

### Cross-platform model

Web/PWA, Windows/Tauri, Android and iOS share the same product core and outcome contracts. Platform adapters implement what the OS legally and technically allows. “Parity” means the best legitimate outcome, not pretending browser code can perform unrestricted native actions. iOS background work and system-wide control, for example, require Apple-supported mechanisms and cannot be treated like an unrestricted desktop runtime.

## User experience model

### Conversation Surface

Default authenticated home. Chat history can hide. Voice can be entered without losing context. New conversation, current project, attachments and compact status remain obvious.

### Dynamic Island

Persistent native compact surface where available. Shows state, progress, approvals, timers, voice, media, handoff and completion; expands only when needed.

### Workspace

A spatial work area for widgets and artifacts. Users can move, resize, overlap, snap, group, stack, pin, dock, minimize and use multi-display layouts.

### Command Palette

The fastest route to any capability, setting, file, agent, project, command, device or action. Search results should be directly actionable.

### Universal Search

Semantic search across the entire user-visible HEY universe, filtered by scope and privacy.

### Home / dashboard

Optional overview of active project, mission, tasks, calendar, weather, prayer, usage, system health and recommendations.

### Trust Center

The place to see and revoke mic/camera/screen/background/device/agent/workflow permissions, cloud/local routing, integrations and recent sensitive actions.

### Tutorial Center

Replayable feature education, teach-by-doing and practice mode so HEY can remain powerful without becoming undiscoverable.

## Personality, modes and communication

HEY can feel brother-like, mentor-like, teacher-like, strategic, creative, critical or execution-focused without changing core truthfulness. Users can control challenge, humor, formality, verbosity, teaching depth, proactive behavior and surprise frequency. Modes should adjust workspace, agent mix, notifications, provider routing and voice/personality together rather than being cosmetic themes.

## Voice: target final experience

Same conversation as text chat; every spoken turn can appear as text and persist.

Continuous hands-free conversation with VAD/turn detection where supported.

Barge-in: user speech interrupts HEY speech quickly and cleanly.

Mute, unmute, stop, end session, output-device selection and visible audio state.

Speech output is sanitized so HEY does not read Markdown syntax, raw URLs, code fences or formatting noise as if they were prose.

Short conversational responses by default, with longer spoken explanations only when useful or requested.

Wake phrase is configurable; the current product preference can ship as “Wake up” while retaining “HEY” as an optional recognizable phrase.

Browser/PWA voice works in the foreground; native apps use platform audio sessions/background mechanisms where browsers cannot provide reliable behavior.

Voice animation reacts to real audio state/levels rather than playing decorative loops unrelated to speech.

## Cosmos: memory and personal intelligence

Cosmos should maintain both a private chronological timeline and a distilled semantic graph. The timeline answers “what happened”; the graph answers “what matters and how is it related.” Neither should mean that the entire memory store is sent to every model call.

Every important memory can carry source/provenance, confidence, timestamps, scope and relationships.

Conflicting memories are detected and resolved or quarantined instead of silently overwriting one another.

Project-isolated memory keeps project context from leaking into unrelated work.

Memory Inbox gives the user a review surface for uncertain or sensitive candidates.

Private Session and local-only modes allow work that should not enter persistent cloud memory.

Time Machine shows how memories, preferences and decisions evolved and what superseded what.

“Never remember this category” and deletion/export controls make memory governance explicit.

## Agents and Forge

The 229 built-in agents are specialist roles selected by orchestration; they should not behave as 229 isolated personalities. The canonical registry drives routing, UI, diagnostics and Forge compatibility. Custom agents remain separate from the built-in count.

Forge is the safe capability expansion system. It can create agents, teams, workflows, skills, commands, automations, widget templates, dashboards, capability packs, adapters and mini-app-like internal capabilities. The lifecycle is requirements → permission design → I/O contract → tests → sandbox/simulation → validation → preview → approval/install → registration → health monitoring → versioning → rollback. Private is the default; sharing is explicit.

## Proposed vNext additions — new capabilities to make HEY better

Everything in this chapter is an extension proposed in this document. These items are not being represented as already implemented. They are designed to strengthen usability, trust, continuity, privacy, creation quality and cross-device behavior while fitting HEY’s existing architecture.

V1. Universal Action Graph — A single graph connecting people, files, apps, devices, projects, agents, permissions, automations and artifacts so HEY can reason about what can be done next without hard-coded navigation.

V2. Intent Layer — A temporary intent object for every meaningful request: goal, constraints, risk, expected proof, deadline, preferred device and privacy level.

V3. Action Rehearsal — For high-impact actions, HEY can simulate the intended sequence and show the exact side effects before execution.

V4. Universal Undo — A cross-feature undo ledger for reversible actions across files, settings, workflows, artifacts and supported app actions.

V5. Proof of Completion — Tasks and missions can define proof requirements such as a changed file hash, sent message ID, created artifact, screenshot, or verified external state.

V6. Consent Receipts — Every sensitive permission or external action can generate a compact receipt showing who/what requested it, why, scope, duration and revocation path.

V7. Data Route Map — A live privacy map showing which information stayed local, which provider saw what context, and why each external route was chosen.

V8. Context Budget — Per-project and per-request controls for how much memory, files, screen content and conversation history may be included.

V9. Zero-Context Share — A one-tap mode that strips personal memory and project context before an external model or shared workspace receives a request.

V10. Private Compute Enclave — When hardware permits, sensitive local processing can be isolated into a constrained local runtime with explicit data-export boundaries.

V11. Shadow Mode — HEY plans what it would do but performs nothing; useful for learning the user, testing automations and auditing risky workflows.

V12. Teach HEY by Correction — When the user corrects an action, HEY can convert the correction into a scoped rule, preference or workflow test instead of repeating the mistake.

V13. Semantic Clipboard — Clipboard history becomes searchable, private-by-default context that can be transformed, compared, cited or moved between trusted devices.

V14. Workspace Scenes — Named multi-widget arrangements such as Launch Day, Study Sprint, Creator Studio and Deep Research, restored per device or display configuration.

V15. Attention Budget — A user-defined daily interruption budget that proactive HEY must respect, with criticality scoring and deferred delivery.

V16. Focus Shield — During focus sessions HEY can suppress noncritical notifications, park incoming tasks, capture interruptions and deliver a structured recap later.

V17. Adaptive Meeting Cockpit — Combines agenda, live notes, action items, relevant project memory, files, participant context and post-meeting follow-up in one mode.

V18. Mission Journal — Long-running missions maintain a human-readable timeline of decisions, attempts, blockers, evidence and recovery points.

V19. What Changed Digest — For projects, files, connected services or devices, HEY can summarize meaningful changes since the user last checked.

V20. Relationship-Aware Memory — Cosmos can distinguish facts about the user, another person, a project, an organization and a device, avoiding accidental cross-contamination.

V21. Memory Counterfactuals — HEY can answer “what would this decision look like if we ignored X preference?” without rewriting stored memory.

V22. Memory Quarantine — Low-confidence or conflicting memories stay isolated until confirmed, instead of silently affecting answers.

V23. Artifact Lineage — Every generated asset can expose its source files, prompts, models/providers, edits, approvals and downstream derivatives.

V24. Design Consistency Compiler — Project DNA can compile brand constraints into machine-checkable rules used by image, document, presentation and UI generation.

V25. Character/Object Identity Vault — Approved references for recurring characters, products and objects can be stored as protected identities with change thresholds.

V26. Multi-Artifact Change Set — One user request can propose coordinated edits across a document, presentation, image set and campaign assets with a single review screen.

V27. Cross-Device Task Migration — A running task can checkpoint and move between desktop, phone, tablet and trusted compute node without restarting the mission.

V28. Proximity Handoff — With explicit opt-in, a task or media session can surface on the most appropriate trusted nearby device.

V29. Room Mode — On supported devices, HEY can operate as an ambient assistant with strong visible sensing indicators, local wake-word processing and strict no-retention defaults.

V30. Multi-Device Camera Director — A project can use multiple trusted camera devices as selectable visual inputs for demonstrations, scanning or guided work.

V31. Compute Pool — Trusted devices can advertise safe compute capabilities so local workloads can be routed based on performance, battery and privacy.

V32. Offline Emergency Pack — A compact local bundle for reminders, critical notes, selected memory, documents, maps/files and basic assistant functions during internet loss.

V33. Provider Arbitration — For high-value tasks, multiple models may independently propose answers and a verifier can select or synthesize using quality/cost/privacy policy.

V34. Provider Reputation Memory — HEY records task-specific provider quality over time rather than relying only on static rankings.

V35. Latency SLOs — Interactive features can declare latency targets; the router chooses a faster fallback when the preferred model is too slow.

V36. Budget Autopilot — Users can set daily/monthly AI budgets; routing automatically adapts quality and provider selection while protecting critical tasks.

V37. Local Model Warm Pool — Frequently used local models can be prewarmed only when power/thermal state permits, avoiding slow first responses without wasting battery.

V38. Trust-Aware Automation — Automations can have trust levels that grow only after successful verified runs and shrink after failures or changed dependencies.

V39. Automation Digital Twin — A workflow can run against mock data and simulated tools before being allowed to touch real systems.

V40. Dependency Watch — HEY monitors workflow/provider/tool dependencies and warns before scheduled missions fail due to expired auth, changed APIs or unavailable devices.

V41. Capability Contracts — Every capability exposes machine-readable inputs, outputs, permissions, risks, platform requirements, fallbacks and verification methods.

V42. Capability Health Map — Users can see Ready, Limited, Needs Setup, Offline or Unavailable states instead of discovering failures during execution.

V43. Safe Self-Expansion — When HEY encounters a missing low-risk capability, Forge can draft and test a candidate; installation still follows risk and approval policy.

V44. Personal Command Language — Users can define natural phrases that map to verified workflows without learning syntax.

V45. Selection Everywhere — Text, files, regions of the screen, browser elements, images or objects can become temporary HEY context through one selection model.

V46. Input Fusion — Voice, text, pointer, camera, screen, gestures and files can be combined in one request while preserving provenance for each input.

V47. Output Fusion — A single task can deliberately produce text, speech, visual overlays, files, widgets, notifications and device actions as one coordinated response.

V48. Live Explain-Why — During execution HEY can answer why a provider, agent, device, permission or action was selected without exposing hidden reasoning.

V49. Confidence Surface — Important factual outputs can display concise confidence/source freshness indicators without cluttering normal chat.

V50. Decision Ledger Plus — Major decisions store alternatives considered, assumptions, evidence, chosen option, review date and later outcome.

V51. Outcome Learning — HEY can ask whether a recommendation or automation actually worked and use that feedback as scoped preference/quality data.

V52. Project Health — Projects get a health layer covering stale decisions, broken links, overdue tasks, unresolved contradictions and unverified outputs.

V53. Research Watchlists — Persistent research questions can be monitored and only notify when a meaningful evidence change occurs.

V54. Source Diffing — For recurring research, HEY highlights what changed between source versions rather than re-summarizing everything.

V55. Evidence Packs — A research result can export a compact bundle containing claims, citations, source snapshots, confidence and unresolved disagreements.

V56. Creator Continuity — Campaigns share approved brand memory, character identity, typography, voice and visual constraints across images, video, motion and copy.

V57. Shot Memory — Video projects remember approved framing, lenses, lighting, movement and continuity rules across generations.

V58. Motion System Memory — Motion timing, easing, transition grammar and typography behavior become reusable Project DNA rather than one-off prompts.

V59. Presentation Runtime — Slides can become live interactive surfaces connected to HEY, notes, timers, audience questions and supporting source material.

V60. Document Live Blocks — Documents can contain refreshable HEY blocks for data, summaries or status sections with explicit provenance and update controls.

V61. Accessibility Autopilot — HEY can proactively detect contrast, focus, captioning, motion and text-size issues in artifacts before export.

V62. Language Identity — Projects can define terminology, tone and translation rules per language rather than treating translation as word substitution.

V63. Religious Source Guard — Religious answers can require explicit source classes/provenance and clearly separate scripture, commentary and uncertain interpretation.

V64. Family / Shared Spaces Firewall — Shared spaces can expose only intentionally shared memory and artifacts while preserving each member’s private Cosmos.

V65. Guest Device Session — A temporary trusted-device session can expire automatically and leave no persistent private memory on the guest device.

V66. Lost Device Kill Switch — Trusted devices can be revoked from the Trust Center, invalidating tokens, handoff keys and background privileges.

V67. Incident Freeze — Emergency Stop can freeze automations, remote control and Forge installs while keeping read-only access to diagnostics and evidence.

V68. Privacy Replay — Users can review a timeline of when mic, camera, screen, local files or external providers were used during a mission.

V69. Release Truth Dashboard — Before launch, public claims are automatically compared against verified evidence so marketing cannot accidentally promise unverified features.

V70. Canary Capability Rollout — New capabilities can ship to a small opt-in group with health gates and automatic rollback conditions.

V71. Self-Test Center — HEY can periodically run non-destructive diagnostics for providers, mic, speakers, camera, notifications, storage, native bridges and database access.

V72. Golden Journeys — Critical user flows such as sign-in → chat → voice → persistence → task execution are continuously tested as release gates.

V73. Session Recovery Capsule — Before risky app upgrades or crashes, HEY can checkpoint open conversations, workspace layout, mission state and unsaved artifact context.

V74. Universal Import — HEY can ingest supported exports from other assistants, notes apps, task managers and file systems into scoped projects without silently merging private data.

V75. Universal Export — Users can export projects, memory, workflows, agents and artifacts into documented open formats to avoid lock-in.

V76. Personal AI Constitution — A user-controlled policy file defines boundaries such as privacy, spending, tone, high-risk actions, proactive behavior and forbidden categories.

V77. Explainable Personalization — HEY can show which explicit preference or project rule changed a response, with one-click correction or disable.

V78. Friction Detector — HEY notices repeated multi-step patterns and suggests an automation only after enough evidence, rather than nagging after one repetition.

V79. Capability Inbox — Newly installed or discovered capabilities appear in a review queue with permissions, examples and suggested placement before cluttering navigation.

V80. Adaptive Navigation — Frequently used capabilities can surface contextually while the primary navigation stays intentionally small and stable.

V81. Command Palette Actions — Search results are actionable: open, summarize, move, share, run, compare, continue, schedule, pin, inspect or ask HEY.

V82. Cross-Surface Continuity — The same object can move from chat to widget to Dynamic Island to notification to device handoff without losing task identity.

V83. Ambient Status Language — Listening, thinking, acting, waiting for approval, offline, degraded and failed states share one consistent visual/audio language everywhere.

V84. Proactive Silence — HEY can decide not to notify when information is low-value, redundant, stale or already handled.

V85. Personal SLA — Users can set expectations such as “never interrupt meetings,” “finish research by morning,” or “prefer privacy over speed,” which become routing policy.

V86. Human Override First — Every autonomous surface keeps a clear stop, pause, cancel, revoke or take-over path appropriate to its risk level.

## Implementation reality snapshot

This section deliberately separates product vision from evidence. It records only facts that have direct evidence from the current project/recent verification, not a blanket “everything works” claim.

Module 00 upgrade foundation: Verified locally. The transactional upgrader supports baseline hashes, backups, conflict detection, redacted logs, resumable state, rollback and local verification gates. Its recorded successful run had 43 tests passing, lint passing, web build passing and Rust cargo check passing.

Chat/auth/persistence: User testing previously confirmed sign-in, normal AI chat, provider response, conversation creation, message persistence, refresh persistence and switching chats. This evidence should not be generalized to unrelated subsystems.

Canonical capability registry: Current source includes a platform-aware registry with supported/unsupported/permission-required/restricted states and adapter-based execution.

Provider registry: Current source includes provider registration plus model/capability listing. Full production multi-provider routing/failover behavior still requires subsystem-specific verification.

Tauri/native desktop: The project contains a Tauri app and native-island window architecture. Successful cargo check verifies compilation in the tested local environment, not every native runtime feature.

Mobile/native verification: Android device behavior, iOS/macOS builds, signed installers and all platform permission flows require their actual environments. These must remain “not tested” until directly verified.

Forge validation: Source architecture includes Forge concepts and validation. “Static validation passed” must not be conflated with executing a generated capability safely in a real sandbox.

## Rules that protect HEY from becoming fake or fragile

Source exists ≠ implemented end-to-end.

Implemented ≠ automated-tested.

Automated-tested ≠ verified working in every platform/environment.

Verified locally ≠ production deployed.

A displayed capability or clickable button must never imply the external action succeeded.

Every public claim should be backed by a current evidence matrix.

Platform constraints should be documented as product behavior, not hidden as bugs or marketing exceptions.

New AI providers and native APIs should be adapters behind stable contracts so HEY does not become coupled to one vendor.

Destructive restructuring must preserve a recoverable backup and rollback path.

## Appendix D — Source basis and reconciliation notes

Primary product basis: the canonical 105-page HEY specification provided by the project owner, containing the complete numbered capability map and agent roster. Additional product decisions in this document reconcile later project directions: Conversation Surface as default home, premium graphite/glass design, one canonical 229-agent registry, free-first launch routing, shared core with native adapters, strong permission boundaries, and evidence-based verification semantics.

Where older directions conflicted, this document favors the newest explicit direction while preserving configurability where possible. Examples: the wake phrase becomes configurable; “Wake up” can be the preferred launch phrase while “HEY” remains an option. Free/Pro/Elite remain architectural plan tiers, while exact commercial pricing is intentionally not hard-coded here. Unreal Engine is not a required product dependency; Dream World or other interactive systems should choose the runtime that best fits the technical requirements.

## Final product statement

HEY should ultimately be the place where the user can think, ask, create, remember, research, decide, automate and act—across files, projects, software and trusted devices—without giving up control over privacy, permissions, proof, reversibility or product quality.


[Table extracted from original Product Bible]

IMPORTANT SCOPE NOTE; This document is a product bible and target specification, not a claim that every capability is already verified in production. “Where supported” means the strongest legitimate implementation permitted by the operating system, connected service, device permissions, provider availability and user authorization. Proposed vNext additions are labeled separately.


[Table extracted from original Product Bible]

Term | Meaning

Canonical / approved | Part of the HEY product specification.

Architected / source exists | The codebase contains an implementation or foundation; this alone is not proof of end-to-end behavior.

Automated-tested | A specific test contract has passed.

Verified working | Direct evidence shows the intended behavior works in the tested environment.

Platform-constrained | The exact behavior depends on OS/API permissions; HEY must use legitimate platform mechanisms or degrade honestly.

Proposed vNext | A new addition in this document intended to make HEY stronger; not represented as already built.
